extracted.intended_audience: educated general public interested in politics, education, and literature (mid-19th century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay assessing the value of speech versus silence, the dangers of sham eloquence, and the proper aims of education and social careers in public life. It argues normative criteria for judging talent, careers, and the role of oratory in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellent silence as a superior test of faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: “excellent silence needed always to accompany excellent speech, and was and is a much rarer and more difficult gift.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence is a rarer and truer sign of human excellence than eloquent speech; one should value the capacity to be silent (endurance, exertion, and good work with lips closed) as a primary marker of worth. The essay contrasts silent, practical apprenticeship learning with mere grammatical utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware sham-excellent speech
rubrics_metrics.description: “really excellent speech ... is terribly apt to get confounded with its counterfeit, sham-excellent ditto,” and “sham-excellent ... deserves to be ranked with the very worst.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse persuasive but false or merely artful speech with genuine wisdom; parliamentary eloquence and popular literature may be admired while being counterfeit. The text warns this counterfeit speech can asphyxiate societies and lead to disastrous consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquent unperformed speech is condemnable
rubrics_metrics.description: “eloquent unperformed speech, in Parliament or elsewhere, is horrible!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech that promises or implies action but is never followed by performance is morally and politically destructive. The essay argues such speech enrolls its practitioner among deceitful, showy figures ('Ignes Fatui') and should be judged harshly—examples include orators who leave their beautiful words as if already done.

rubrics_metrics.name: True education must produce inward capital, not just facility of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech should be 'the bank-note of an inward capital of culture'; if there is no inward capital, speech is a forged note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate education by whether it creates substantial intellectual and moral content (the 'bullion') rather than merely training people to utter clever phrases. The analogy highlights social harm when eloquence circulates without underlying competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship/practical training over grammar-as-end
rubrics_metrics.description: The old rule: learn the business by apprenticeship; the schoolmaster teaching mere speaking was secondary and parasitic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer and value practical apprenticeship and hands-on mastery ('the Working Man' learning by ploughing and hammering) as the primary route to competence. Formal grammar and rhetorical drills should be a supplement, not the core of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society should select doers, not merely talkers, for high office
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of questions: How do men rise in your Society? What kind of men—noble gifts or ignoble? The essay criticizes choosing leaders primarily by their powers of talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection criteria for public office should emphasize proven action and inward worth rather than eloquent proof-feats. Reliance on speech-as-proof (parliamentary speeches, stump-oratory) produces folly and risks anarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The art of speech can be corrupting if it substitutes for real work
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Art of Speech is probably definable in that case as the short summary of all the Black Arts put together.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When speech becomes the dominant form of education and social proof, it functions as a finishing workshop for deceit, making polished falsehoods marketable. This warns evaluators to distrust rhetoric that substitutes for competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honest industrial 'beaverism' from dishonest 'vulpine' careers
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'beaver career' (honest contrivance, accumulation of capital, engineering and machinery) vs the 'vulpine' (inhuman and dishonest) career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising or judging career paths, encourage honest industrial work which, while silent, can be morally respectable and socially valuable; condemn careers that pursue dishonesty or mere cunning for gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silent industrial careers have moral and civic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Many silent industrials (mill-owners, agricultural, commercial, mechanical) appear to the author more developed men than some high-speaking individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate individuals by their productive, sustained contributions (industry, craft) even if they lack rhetorical gifts; such lives may realize 'half the result' (national wealth) and deserve honor when guided by wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: The current social test of excellence—dexterous talk—is a flawed selection mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of excellence is to be done by the tongue: 'Contrive to talk well, you will get to Heaven... Do not talk well, only work well, and heroically hold your peace, you have no chance whatever to get thither.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique social institutions that reward rhetorical agility as the main qualification for leadership. The essay suggests alternative proof-feats and implies selection should incorporate other demonstrations of ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public eloquence often masks unveracity and expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on 'Hansard's Debates' and 'lamentable unveracities uttered in Parliament... talking from the teeth outward, not as the convictions but as the expediencies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging speeches or parliamentary rhetoric, be alert to speech given for expediency rather than conviction; treat such unveracity as a significant negative criterion in evaluating politicians and public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'stump-orator' as an anti-pattern: admired for wind rather than substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'excellent Stump-orator' is often 'merely the windiest mortal of them all' and admired wrongly; he functions as a 'mouthpiece of Chaos.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an anti-pattern to identify rhetoricians whose appeal is style over substance. In evaluating orators, prioritize demonstrable insight, truthfulness, and capacity to act over mere crowd-pleasing oratory.
